{{short description|Sufficiently long sequences of numbers have long monotonic subsequences}}
[[Image:Monotone-subseq-17-5.svg|thumb|upright=1.35|A path of four upward-sloping edges in a set of 17 points. By the Erdős–Szekeres theorem, every set of 17 points has a path of this length that slopes either upward or downward.  The 16-point subset with the central point removed has no such path.]]
In [[mathematics]], the '''Erdős–Szekeres theorem''' asserts that, given <math>r</math> and <math>s</math>, any sequence of distinct real numbers with length at least <math>(r-1)(s-1)+1</math> contains a monotonically increasing subsequence of length&nbsp;''r'' ''or'' a monotonically decreasing subsequence of length&nbsp;''s''. The proof appeared in the same 1935 paper that mentions the [[Happy Ending problem]].<ref>{{Citation
  | authorlink1 = Paul Erdős | last1 = Erdős | first1 = Paul | authorlink2 = George Szekeres | last2 = Szekeres | first2 = George
  | title = A combinatorial problem in geometry
  | journal = [[Compositio Mathematica]]
  | volume = 2
  | pages = 463–470
  | year = 1935
  | url = http://www.numdam.org/item?id=CM_1935__2__463_0
  | zbl = 0012.27010}}; reprinted in ''Classic Papers in Combinatorics'' (Springer, 2008), pp. 49–56, {{doi|10.1007/978-0-8176-4842-8_3}}, {{isbn|978-0-8176-4841-1}}</ref> 

It is a finitary result that makes precise one of the corollaries of [[Ramsey's theorem]].  While Ramsey's theorem makes it easy to prove that every infinite sequence of distinct real numbers contains a monotonically increasing infinite [[subsequence]] ''or'' a monotonically decreasing infinite subsequence, the result proved by [[Paul Erdős]] and [[George Szekeres]] goes further. 

== Example ==
For ''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3 and ''s''&nbsp;=&nbsp;2, the formula tells us that any permutation of three numbers has an increasing subsequence of length three or a decreasing subsequence of length two. Among the six permutations of the numbers 1,2,3:
* <math>\langle1,2,3\rangle</math> has an increasing subsequence consisting of all three numbers.
* <math>\langle1,3,2\rangle</math> has a decreasing subsequence <math>\langle3,2\rangle</math>
* <math>\langle2,1,3\rangle</math> has a decreasing subsequence <math>\langle2,1\rangle</math>
* <math>\langle2,3,1\rangle</math> has two decreasing subsequences, <math>\langle2,1\rangle</math> and <math>\langle3,1\rangle</math>
* <math>\langle3,1,2\rangle</math> has two decreasing subsequences, <math>\langle3,1\rangle</math> and <math>\langle3,2\rangle</math>
* <math>\langle3,2,1\rangle</math> has three decreasing length-2 subsequences, <math>\langle3,2\rangle</math>, <math>\langle3,1\rangle</math> and <math>\langle2,1\rangle</math>.

== Alternative interpretations ==
=== Geometric interpretation ===
One can interpret the positions of the numbers in a sequence as ''x''-coordinates of points in the [[Euclidean plane]], and the numbers themselves as ''y''-coordinates; conversely, for any point set in the plane, the ''y''-coordinates of the points, ordered by their ''x''-coordinates, forms a sequence of numbers (unless two of the points have equal ''x''-coordinates).  With this translation between sequences and point sets, the Erdős–Szekeres theorem can be interpreted as stating that in any set of at least ''rs''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''r''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''s''&nbsp;+&nbsp;2 points we can find a [[polygonal path]] of either ''r''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 positive-slope edges or ''s''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 negative-slope edges. In particular (taking ''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''s''), in any set of at least ''n'' points we can find a polygonal path of at least ⌊{{radic|''n''-1}}⌋ edges with same-sign slopes. For instance, taking ''r''&nbsp;=&nbsp;''s''&nbsp;=&nbsp;5, any set of at least 17 points has a four-edge path in which all slopes have the same sign.

An example of ''rs''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''r''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;''s''&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 points without such a path, showing that this bound is tight, can be formed by applying a small rotation to an (''r''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)-by-(''s''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1) grid.

=== Permutation pattern interpretation ===
The Erdős–Szekeres theorem may also be interpreted in the language of [[permutation pattern]]s as stating that every permutation of length at least (''r''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)(''s''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)&nbsp;+&nbsp;1 must contain the pattern 12⋯''r'' or the pattern ''s''⋯21.

===Pigeonhole principle===
Given a sequence of length (''r''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)(''s''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)&nbsp;+&nbsp;1, label each number ''n<sub>i</sub>'' in the sequence with the pair (''a<sub>i</sub>'', ''b<sub>i</sub>''), where ''a<sub>i</sub>'' is the length of the longest monotonically increasing subsequence ending with ''n<sub>i</sub>'' and ''b<sub>i</sub>'' is the length of the longest monotonically decreasing subsequence ending with ''n<sub>i</sub>''. Each two numbers in the sequence are labeled with a different pair: if {{nowrap|''i'' < ''j''}} and {{nowrap|''n<sub>i</sub>'' < ''n<sub>j</sub>''}} then {{nowrap|''a<sub>i</sub>'' < ''a<sub>j</sub>''}}, and on the other hand if {{nowrap|''n<sub>i</sub>'' > ''n<sub>j</sub>''}} then {{nowrap|''b<sub>i</sub>'' < ''b<sub>j</sub>''}}. But there are only (''r''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1)(''s''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1) possible labels if ''a<sub>i</sub>'' is at most ''r''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 and ''b<sub>i</sub>'' is at most ''s''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1, so by the [[pigeonhole principle]] there must exist a value of ''i'' for which ''a<sub>i</sub>'' or ''b<sub>i</sub>'' is outside this range. If ''a<sub>i</sub>'' is out of range then ''n<sub>i</sub>'' is part of an increasing sequence of length at least ''r'', and if ''b<sub>i</sub>'' is out of range then ''n<sub>i</sub>'' is part of a decreasing sequence of length at least ''s''.

{{harvtxt|Steele|1995}} credits this proof to the one-page paper of {{harvtxt|Seidenberg|1959}} and calls it "the slickest and most systematic" of the proofs he surveys.<ref name="steele"/><ref>{{citation
 | last = Seidenberg | first = A. | authorlink = Abraham Seidenberg
 | journal = [[Journal of the London Mathematical Society]]
 | page = 352
 | title = A simple proof of a theorem of Erdős and Szekeres
 | volume = 34
 | year = 1959
 | issue = 3 | doi = 10.1112/jlms/s1-34.3.352 }}</ref>

===Dilworth's theorem===
Another of the proofs uses [[Dilworth's theorem]] on chain decompositions in partial orders, or its simpler dual ([[Mirsky's theorem]]).

To prove the theorem, define a partial ordering on the members of the sequence, in which ''x'' is less than or equal to ''y'' in the partial order if ''x''&nbsp;≤&nbsp;''y'' as numbers and ''x'' is not later than ''y'' in the sequence.  A chain in this partial order is a monotonically increasing subsequence, and an [[antichain]] is a monotonically decreasing subsequence. By Mirsky's theorem, either there is a chain of length ''r'', or the sequence can be partitioned into at most ''r''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 antichains; but in that case the largest of the antichains must form a decreasing subsequence with length at least
:<math>\left\lceil\frac{rs-r-s+2}{r-1}\right\rceil=s.</math>

Alternatively, by Dilworth's theorem itself, either there is an antichain of length ''s'', or the sequence can be partitioned into at most ''s''&nbsp;&minus;&nbsp;1 chains, the longest of which must have length at least&nbsp;''r''.

=== Application of the Robinson–Schensted correspondence ===
The result can also be obtained as a corollary of the [[Robinson–Schensted correspondence]].

Recall that the Robinson–Schensted correspondence associates to each sequence a [[Young tableau]] ''P'' whose entries are the values of the sequence. The tableau ''P'' has the following properties: 

* The length of the longest increasing subsequence is equal to the length of the first row of ''P''.
* The length of the longest decreasing subsequence is equal to the length of the first column of ''P''.

Now, it is not possible to fit (''r''&thinsp;−&thinsp;1)(''s''&thinsp;−&thinsp;1) + 1 entries in a square box of size (''r''&thinsp;−&thinsp;1)(''s''&thinsp;−&thinsp;1), so that either the first row is of length at least ''r'' or the first column is of length at least ''s''.
